fuentes/historia-natural-y-moral-de-las-.texto: Natural and Moral History of the Indies

A treatise by the Jesuit José de Acosta in seven books: the first deal with the sky, climate, and land of America; the following with metals, plants, and animals; the last with religion, government, and the history of the Incas and the Mexica. He proposes that the first inhabitants reached America by land from the north, describes the altitude sickness he suffered when crossing the cordillera at Pariacaca, and explains the mercury-based exploitation of silver at Potosí. For the Incas he uses the reports of Polo de Ondegardo; for the Mexica, the manuscript of the Jesuit Juan de Tovar.

It was one of the most widely read works on America in Europe at the end of the 16th century and was soon translated into several languages. Its explanation of Indigenous religions as a demonic imitation of the sacraments coexists with a favorable judgment of the government of the Incas and the Mexica, which it holds up as an example of political order.
Old edition, volume 1, on Internet Archive

fuentes/de-procuranda-indorum-salute/tit.texto: De procuranda indorum salute (On How to Promote the Salvation of the Indians)

fuentes/de-procuranda-indorum-salute/res.texto: A treatise on the evangelization of the Indians, written in Lima and published in Salamanca. In its preface it distinguishes three classes of “barbarians” according to their level of government and writing: it places the Chinese and Japanese in the first, the Incas and the Mexica in the second, and peoples without cities or laws in the third. It argues that the faith must be taught in the Indians’ language and through persuasion, criticizes the abuses of encomenderos, corregidores, and doctrinal priests, and discusses the lawfulness of wars of conquest and of forced labor.

fuentes/de-procuranda-indorum-salute/por.texto: It is one of the main Jesuit works on the evangelization of America and one of the foundations of the Third Council of Lima (1582-1583), of which Acosta was a theologian.

fuentes/manuscrito-de-huarochiri/autor.texto: Anonymous (compiled at the request of Francisco de Ávila)

fuentes/manuscrito-de-huarochiri/soporte.texto: Untitled manuscript that begins “Runa yndio ñiscap machoncuna” (National Library of Spain, ms. 3169)

fuentes/manuscrito-de-huarochiri/resumen.texto: The only extensive Quechua text from the early colonial period that recounts the traditions of an Andean province from the point of view of its inhabitants: the myths of Pariacaca and Cuniraya Viracocha, the wars of the Yauyos, who came down from the highlands against the Yuncas of the valleys, the cult of the huacas and ancestors, festivals and offerings, and the relationship of these peoples with the Incas. It was written by one or more Christianized Andeans from the highlands of Lima at the request of the priest Francisco de Ávila, who used it in his campaign against “idolatries”; some scholars propose as source or author Cristóbal Choquecasa, a local noble who appears in the text.

fuentes/manuscrito-de-huarochiri/por_que.texto: It is the main source in an Andean language on the religion of the period before the conquest. It was translated by Hermann Trimborn (1939), José María Arguedas (1966), Gerald Taylor (1987), and Frank Salomon and George Urioste (1991).

fuentes/manuscrito-de-huarochiri/leer.0..texto: Francisco de Ávila’s treatise (1608) based on the first chapters of the manuscript, in Markham’s English translation (1873), on Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-del-nuevo-mundo-cobo/so.texto: Manuscript, published in Seville in 1890-1895 by Marcos Jiménez de la Espada

fuentes/historia-del-nuevo-mundo-cobo/re.texto: A work finished in Lima in 1653, of which only the first part survives: the natural world of America (sky, minerals, plants, and animals, with many species described with precision) and a history and description of the Incas, their religion, government, and customs. It copies the list of 328 huacas of Cusco arranged in ceques, taken from a lost text that many scholars attribute to Polo de Ondegardo, and uses chronicles that no longer survive.

fuentes/historia-del-nuevo-mundo-cobo/po.texto: For its method and care, it is the most complete colonial description of Inca religion and society and the basis of the modern study of the ceque system.

fuentes/historia-del-nuevo-mundo-cobo/le.texto: Marcos Jiménez de la Espada edition (Seville, 1890), volume 1, on Internet Archive

fuentes/relacion-de-las-fabulas-y-ritos/.texto: Account of the Fables and Rites of the Incas

A report written for the bishop of Cusco, Sebastián de Lartaún. It records the origin myths of Titicaca and Pacaritambo, Inca prayers in Quechua with their translation, the ritual calendar month by month, the festival of Citua to expel illness from the city, and the capacocha, with the sending of children and offerings from Cusco to the huacas of the provinces to be sacrificed. At the end it describes the Taki Onqoy movement of the 1560s.
It is one of the earliest and most detailed sources on the rites of Cusco, drawn from elders who had served in the Inca cult, and the one that best preserves Quechua prayers from before the conquest.
English translation by Clements Markham (Hakluyt Society, 1873), on Internet Archive

fuentes/historia-general-del-piru-murua/.texto: Illustrated manuscripts: the Galvin (1590, private collection) and the Getty (1616, J. Paul Getty Museum)

A chronicle on the origin, kings, coyas, laws, rites, and customs of the Incas, and on the conquest, of which there are two versions: the first, titled Historia del origen y genealogía real de los reyes incas del Perú (1590), and the definitive one of 1616, approved for printing but left unpublished. Many of the illustrations in the first are by Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala.
The two manuscripts show how a colonial chronicle was made, with collaboration and conflict between a Spanish friar and an Andean author, and preserve images of Inca clothing and offices.

fuentes/miscelanea-antartica/soporte.texto: Manuscript, published in partial French translation in 1840 and in Spanish in 1951

fuentes/miscelanea-antartica/resumen.texto: A universal history written in Quito whose third part deals with Peru: the origin of the Indians, the Inca kings with dates for each reign, Huayna Cápac’s wars in the north (including the massacre at Yahuarcocha), the civil war, and the arrival of the Spaniards. It preserves the legend of Naylamp, who supposedly arrived by sea at Lambayeque with his court and founded a dynasty.

fuentes/miscelanea-antartica/por_que_imp.texto: Its dates for the Inca reigns, whose origin is unknown, are those John Rowe adopted in 1945 and have been repeated ever since (Pachacútec from 1438); radiocarbon dates suggest an earlier expansion.

fuentes/relacion-de-las-costumbres-antig.texto: Account of the Ancient Customs of the Natives of Peru
Manuscript, published in 1879 by Marcos Jiménez de la Espada

An anonymous treatise on the religion, temples, priests, consecrated virgins, and laws of the Incas. It argues that the Incas worshipped a single creator god, of whom the Sun and the huacas were intermediaries, and it denies or minimizes their human sacrifices, which it attributes to errors by the Spaniards or to other peoples. Since the late 19th century it has been attributed to Blas Valera, an attribution that many accept and others dispute.

Together with the passages from Valera that Garcilaso cites, it is the basis of the image of almost monotheistic Incas without human sacrifice, an image that contradicts other chronicles (Betanzos, Molina, Cobo) and the archaeology of the capacocha.

fuentes/historia-del-reino-de-quito/titu.texto: History of the Kingdom of Quito in South America

fuentes/historia-del-reino-de-quito/resu.texto: A natural, ancient, and modern history of the Audiencia of Quito, written in exile. It narrates a “kingdom of Quito” ruled by the shyris, a people who supposedly arrived by sea, conquered the highlands around the year 1000, and dominated them until the Inca conquest; their heiress, Paccha, supposedly married Huayna Cápac and was the mother of Atahualpa. It claims to rest on sources that no longer survive, among them a writing by Fray Marcos de Niza.

fuentes/historia-del-reino-de-quito/por_.texto: It was the basis of Ecuadorian national history in the 19th century and of school teaching. Since Jacinto Jijón y Caamaño’s critique (1918), most historians and archaeologists regard the kingdom of the shyris as a construction without documentary or archaeological support, although it retains defenders.

fuentes/historia-del-reino-de-quito/leer.texto: Volume II (ancient history) of the Quito edition of 1841, on Internet Archive

fuentes/visita-de-chucuito-1567/titulo.texto: Inspection of the Province of Chucuito by Garci Diez de San Miguel in 1567

fuentes/visita-de-chucuito-1567/soporte.texto: Inspection file, published in Lima in 1964

fuentes/visita-de-chucuito-1567/resumen.texto: An inspection of the province of the lupacas, on the shores of Lake Titicaca, which the Crown held in its own encomienda. The inspector questioned the two principal lords, Martín Cari and Martín Cusi, and other curacas about the population, the tribute and services they gave the Inca and those they gave the Spaniards, the herds of llamas and alpacas, and the lands they held on the Pacific coast and in the eastern valleys, many days’ journey away.

fuentes/visita-de-chucuito-1567/por_que_.texto: It is one of the sources on which John Murra based the model of the “vertical archipelago,” and it shows how a great Aymara lordship worked before and after 1532.

fuentes/visita-de-huanuco-1562/titulo.texto: Inspection of the Province of León de Huánuco in 1562

fuentes/visita-de-huanuco-1562/soporte.texto: Inspection file, published in Huánuco in 1967-1972 with studies by John Murra

fuentes/visita-de-huanuco-1562/resumen.texto: A house-by-house inspection of the Chupachos and other groups of the Huánuco region, carried out to set their tribute. It records who lived in each dwelling, what they produced, and what services they had provided to the Inca: guards, weavers, mitmaqs sent to other regions, porters, and workers for the storehouses of Huánuco Pampa. The second volume includes Murra’s essay on the vertical control of ecological floors.

fuentes/visita-de-huanuco-1562/por_que_i.texto: It allows the Cusco-based chronicles’ accounts of the mita and Inca redistribution to be compared from below, with data from each community.

fuentes/aviso-de-chincha/titulo.texto: Notice on the Manner of Government of the Indians in the Time of the Inga

fuentes/aviso-de-chincha/soporte.texto: Manuscript, published in 1970 by María Rostworowski

fuentes/aviso-de-chincha/resumen.texto: A short anonymous report on the Chincha valley that claims that before the conquest there were 30,000 tributaries there, among them 12,000 farmers, 10,000 fishermen, and 6,000 merchants who traded with Cusco, the Collao, and Quito. María Rostworowski used it to argue that Chincha was a lordship of seafaring merchants with long-distance exchange.

fuentes/aviso-de-chincha/por_que_importa.texto: It is one of the few sources describing specialized trade in the Andes, where merchants were supposed not to exist; its figures, like those of all reports of its kind, should be read with caution.

fuentes/absolute-chronology-rowe/titulo.texto: Absolute Chronology in the Andean Area

fuentes/absolute-chronology-rowe/resumen.texto: An article in which John Rowe proposed absolute dates for the Inca reigns based on the chronology of Miguel Cabello Balboa: Pachacútec supposedly began to reign in 1438, Topa Inca in 1471, and Huayna Cápac in 1493. Rowe presented them as approximate, but textbooks adopted them as firm.

fuentes/absolute-chronology-rowe/por_que.texto: It is the origin of the short chronology of the Inca Empire, which has been under review since radiocarbon dates from Machu Picchu, Cusco, and the Collasuyo suggest that the expansion began decades earlier.

fuentes/inca-culture-rowe/titulo.texto: Inca Culture at the Time of the Spanish Conquest

fuentes/inca-culture-rowe/soporte.texto: Chapter in the Handbook of South American Indians, vol. 2 (Smithsonian Institution)

fuentes/inca-culture-rowe/resumen.texto: A synthesis of Inca society, economy, religion, warfare, and history based on a critical reading of the chronicles, which privileges early and well-informed authors. It estimates the population of the empire around 1525 at about six million people.

fuentes/inca-culture-rowe/por_que_import.texto: For decades it was the standard description of Inca culture and established many of the categories with which it is still studied.

fuentes/formaciones-economicas-murra/tit.texto: Economic and Political Formations of the Andean World

fuentes/formaciones-economicas-murra/res.texto: A collection of essays that read the administrative inspections of the 16th century alongside the chronicles. It includes “The Vertical Control of a Maximum of Ecological Floors,” in which Murra proposes that Andean groups maintained colonies at different altitudes, sometimes days’ journey away, to obtain products of the puna, the valleys, and the coast without depending on exchange; and studies of reciprocity, state redistribution, textiles, and maize in the Inca economy.

fuentes/formaciones-economicas-murra/por.texto: The “vertical archipelago” and the economy of reciprocity and redistribution became central to Andean ethnohistory; later it was debated how far they hold for the coast, where María Rostworowski documented merchants and specialists.

fuentes/historia-del-tahuantinsuyu/resum.texto: A history of the Inca state based on chronicles and archival documents, which presents the Incas as one lordship among others that imposed itself through war and through pacts of reciprocity and kinship with the curacas. It argues that succession did not follow a fixed rule of primogeniture and was often resolved by fighting between brothers, which explains the war between Huáscar and Atahualpa.

fuentes/historia-del-tahuantinsuyu/por_q.texto: It was a reference text in Peru and Latin America and helped view the Tawantinsuyu from the lordships and not only from Cusco.

fuentes/the-incas-daltroy/soporte.texto: Book (Blackwell, The Peoples of America series; second edition 2015)

fuentes/the-incas-daltroy/resumen.texto: An archaeological and historical synthesis of the Inca Empire: its origins in Cusco, its expansion, the economy of state lands and storehouses, labor by rotation, the mitmaqs, the royal road, and the administration of the provinces, with data from the excavations in the Mantaro Valley that the author directed.

fuentes/the-incas-daltroy/por_que_import.texto: It is one of the most widely used university textbooks on the Incas and shows an empire that combined force with negotiation with local elites.

fuentes/ceque-system-zuidema/titulo.texto: The Ceque System of Cuzco: The Social Organization of the Capital of the Inca

fuentes/ceque-system-zuidema/resumen.texto: An analysis of the list of Cusco’s huacas arranged in ceques preserved by Cobo, from which Zuidema deduces that this system organized kinship, the calendar, irrigation, and the hierarchy of the city’s groups. He argues that the lists of Inca kings in the chronicles are not a historical succession but a representation of social structure, and that there may have been a dual government.

fuentes/ceque-system-zuidema/por_que_imp.texto: It opened the structural reading of Inca history, which many historians dispute because it strips the chronicles of historical value, and it was the starting point for fieldwork on the ceques.

fuentes/the-chanka-bauer/titulo.texto: The Chanka: Archaeological Research in Andahuaylas (Apurimac), Peru

fuentes/the-chanka-bauer/autor.texto: Brian S. Bauer, Lucas C. Kellett, and Miriam Aráoz Silva

fuentes/the-chanka-bauer/resumen.texto: A report of a systematic archaeological survey of the Andahuaylas region, land of the Chanka according to the chronicles. For the period before the Incas it recorded hilltop villages with defensive walls and ditches, and no major political center.

fuentes/the-chanka-bauer/por_que_importa.texto: Its authors conclude that the Chanka were dispersed and conflicting groups, not the state capable of threatening Cusco that the chronicles describe, which supports reading the war against the Chanka as a legitimizing account of Pachacútec.

fuentes/how-the-incas-built-their-heartl.texto: How the Incas Built Their Heartland: State Formation and the Innovation of Imperial Strategies in the Sacred Valley, Peru

An archaeological study of the Cusco valley and the Sacred Valley according to which the Inca state formed over several centuries, from around the year 1000, through marriage alliances, wars, and the absorption of neighboring groups, before the great expansion that the chronicles attribute to Pachacútec.
Together with the radiocarbon dates, it challenges the account of an empire that arose all at once after the war against the Chanka.

fuentes/reading-inca-history/resumen.texto: An analysis of the chronicles on the Incas that seeks to reconstruct the Andean historical genres from which they derive (genealogies, life accounts of each Inca, records in quipu) and to separate what comes from them from what the Spanish chroniclers added.

fuentes/reading-inca-history/por_que_imp.texto: It is one of the foundations of the critical use of the chronicles as a source for Inca history.

fuentes/dating-caral/titulo.texto: Dating Caral, a Preceramic Site in the Supe Valley on the Central Coast of Peru

fuentes/dating-caral/soporte.texto: Article (Science, vol. 292), with Jonathan Haas and Winifred Creamer

fuentes/dating-caral/resumen.texto: Published the first radiocarbon dates for Caral, which placed its monumental architecture between approximately 2600 and 2000 BC and made it one of the oldest urban centers in the Americas.

fuentes/dating-caral/por_que_importa.texto: It showed that the Andes had monumental architecture and urban life before pottery, in inland valleys and not only on the seashore.

fuentes/maritime-foundations-moseley/tit.texto: The Maritime Foundations of Andean Civilization

fuentes/maritime-foundations-moseley/res.texto: He proposes that Andean civilization originated in coastal villages that lived from fishing and shellfish gathering, and that they were able to raise monumental architecture before intensive agriculture, thanks to the richness of the sea off Peru.

fuentes/maritime-foundations-moseley/por.texto: The maritime hypothesis was much debated; the finds at Caral and in the Norte Chico qualified it with an economy that combined fishing with cotton and valley crops.

fuentes/chavin-burger/titulo.texto: Chavín and the Origins of Andean Civilization

fuentes/chavin-burger/resumen.texto: A synthesis of the archaeology of the central Andes from the Archaic to the end of the Early Horizon, centered on Chavín de Huántar, where the author excavated. He interprets Chavín as a cult center whose religion spread through the highlands and coast between 900 and 200 BC, rather than as a conquering state.

fuentes/chavin-burger/por_que_importa.texto: It is the modern reference work on Chavín; later excavations, such as those of John Rick, proposed earlier dates for the temple.

fuentes/chavin-tello/titulo.texto: Chavín: Mother Culture of Andean Civilization

fuentes/chavin-tello/soporte.texto: Posthumous book, edited by Toribio Mejía Xesspe (National University of San Marcos)

fuentes/chavin-tello/resumen.texto: It gathers Tello’s research from 1919 on Chavín de Huántar and related sites and argues that Chavín was the mother culture of Andean civilization, with roots in the highlands and the Amazon, and not a derivative of influences that arrived from Mesoamerica.

fuentes/chavin-tello/por_que_importa.texto: It established the idea of an autochthonous origin for Andean civilization, against Uhle’s diffusionist theory; later finds of older sites, such as Caral, qualified it.

fuentes/pachacamac-uhle/titulo.texto: Pachacamac: Report of the William Pepper, M.D., LL.D., Peruvian Expedition of 1896

fuentes/pachacamac-uhle/resumen.texto: A report on the 1896 excavations at the Pachacamac sanctuary, with its cemeteries, the Inca Temple of the Sun, and the ancient temple of the local deity. Uhle arranged the tombs by strata and pottery styles and distinguished styles earlier than the Incas, among them one related to that of Tiwanaku.

fuentes/pachacamac-uhle/por_que_importa.texto: It was the first stratigraphic study of an Andean site and the basis of the cultural sequence that still organizes Peruvian archaeology.

fuentes/royal-tombs-of-sipan/soporte.texto: Book, with Christopher B. Donnan (Fowler Museum of Cultural History, UCLA)

fuentes/royal-tombs-of-sipan/resumen.texto: A publication of the 1987-1990 excavations at Huaca Rajada, Sipán: the tomb of the Lord of Sipán, that of the so-called priest, and that of the old lord of Sipán, with their grave goods of gold, silver, copper, shells, and textiles and the people buried with them. It identifies the buried individuals with the figures of the “sacrifice ceremony” in Moche painting.

fuentes/royal-tombs-of-sipan/por_que_imp.texto: It showed that the figures in that iconography were offices held by real people.

fuentes/physical-evidence-sacrifice-vera.texto: The Physical Evidence of Human Sacrifice in Ancient Peru
Chapter in Ritual Sacrifice in Ancient Peru, edited by Elizabeth P. Benson and Anita G. Cook (University of Texas Press)

A review of the skeletal evidence of human sacrifice in the Andes, from the trophy heads of Nazca and the victims of the Moche Huaca de la Luna to Inca offerings: throat cuttings, dismemberment, cut marks, and healed and unhealed fractures. It distinguishes cases in which the record proves sacrifice from those in which only iconography suggests it.
It is one of the foundations of the archaeological study of sacrifice in the Andes and the reference on the victims of the Huaca de la Luna, whom Verano interprets as prisoners of war.

fuentes/holes-in-the-head/titulo.texto: Holes in the Head: The Art and Archaeology of Trepanation in Ancient Peru

fuentes/holes-in-the-head/resumen.texto: A study of more than 800 trepanned skulls from the Andes, from Paracas to the Incas. It shows that the operation was done mainly to treat fractures and other skull injuries, and that the share of patients who survived, measured by bone regeneration, grew over time to exceed three quarters in Inca times.

fuentes/holes-in-the-head/por_que_import.texto: Documents one of the most developed surgical practices of the ancient world.

fuentes/huanchaquito-prieto-2019/titulo.texto: A mass sacrifice of children and camelids at the Huanchaquito-Las Llamas site, Moche Valley, Peru

fuentes/huanchaquito-prieto-2019/autor.texto: Gabriel Prieto, John W. Verano and others

fuentes/huanchaquito-prieto-2019/resumen.texto: Publishes the excavations of 2011, 2014 and 2016 at a coastal site near Chan Chan, where 137 children and adolescents aged 5 to 14 (the article’s abstract rounds this up to more than 140), three adults and about 200 young camelids were buried in a single episode, around 1450. The children have cuts on the sternum and separated ribs, a sign that their chests were opened, perhaps to remove the heart. Preliminary DNA shows that there were both boys and girls, and cranial deformation and isotopes suggest they came from different regions and groups. Footprints in the mud show that they were led in procession after heavy rains, and the authors propose linking the sacrifice to an El Niño episode.

fuentes/huanchaquito-prieto-2019/por_que.texto: According to its authors, it is the largest known mass sacrifice of children and camelids in the Americas; it shows that the Chimú state carried out mass sacrifices before the Inca conquest.

fuentes/inca-rituals-and-sacred-mountain.texto: Inca Rituals and Sacred Mountains: A Study of the World's Highest Archaeological Sites
Book, with Constanza Ceruti (Cotsen Institute of Archaeology, UCLA)

An inventory of Inca high-mountain shrines, on summits above 5,000 meters in Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Argentina, with the results of the authors’ excavations on Ampato, Llullaillaco and other volcanoes: platforms, offerings of figurines, textiles and food, and the bodies of children sacrificed in the capacocha.
Brings together the archaeological basis of what is known about the capacocha and the Inca cult of mountains.

fuentes/wilson-2013-capacocha/titulo.texto: Archaeological, radiological, and biological evidence offer insight into Inca child sacrifice

fuentes/wilson-2013-capacocha/soporte.texto: Article (Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, vol. 110, no. 33)

fuentes/wilson-2013-capacocha/resumen.texto: An archaeological, radiological and biological study of the three children of Llullaillaco: a girl of about 13 and a boy and a girl aged 4 to 5. Analysis of their hair, segment by segment, indicates rising consumption of coca and alcohol before death; in the eldest, coca use rose sharply about a year earlier and alcohol peaked in her final weeks, and the CT scan showed that she died with a wad of coca in her mouth. The authors propose that these substances were part of the ritual and served to sedate her, and that each child was treated according to age, rank and role in the rite.

fuentes/wilson-2013-capacocha/por_que_im.texto: Provides biological data on how the victims of the capacocha were prepared, which the chronicles described only in general terms.

fuentes/tiwanaku-kolata/titulo.texto: The Tiwanaku: Portrait of an Andean Civilization

fuentes/tiwanaku-kolata/resumen.texto: A synthesis of the author’s excavations at Tiahuanaco and Lukurmata since 1978. It presents Tiahuanaco as the capital of a centralized state supported by raised fields on the shore of Lake Titicaca and by colonies in lower valleys such as Moquegua and Cochabamba, and attributes its collapse, around 1000–1100, to a prolonged drought.

fuentes/tiwanaku-kolata/por_que_importa.texto: His model of a centralized state that collapsed because of drought was very influential and much debated: other archaeologists see Tiahuanaco as a less centralized religious and political center.

fuentes/huari-administrative-structure/t.texto: Huari Administrative Structure: Prehistoric Monumental Architecture and State Government

fuentes/huari-administrative-structure/a.texto: William H. Isbell and Gordon F. McEwan (editors)

fuentes/huari-administrative-structure/r.texto: Proceedings of a symposium on the large orthogonal enclosures of Huari, Pikillacta, Viracochapampa and other sites, in which Isbell, McEwan, Katharina Schreiber and others argue that they were administrative centers of an expansive state with its capital at Huari, a precursor of the Inca Empire.

fuentes/huari-administrative-structure/p.texto: Set the terms of the debate between those who see Huari as an empire with provincial administration and those who see it as a network of centers of religious and commercial influence.

fuentes/violence-ritual-wari-tung/titulo.texto: Violence, Ritual, and the Wari Empire: A Social Bioarchaeology of Imperialism in the Ancient Andes

fuentes/violence-ritual-wari-tung/resume.texto: A study of skeletons from Conchopata, near the Huari capital, and from Beringa, in the Majes Valley: skull injuries in men, women and children, and trophy heads prepared to be hung, many of them from people who were not local according to isotope analysis. It concludes that warfare, the capture of enemies and the display of trophies were part of Wari expansion.

fuentes/violence-ritual-wari-tung/por_qu.texto: It is the main bioarchaeological evidence of violence associated with the Wari state.

fuentes/interpreting-conflict-arkush-sta.texto: Interpreting Conflict in the Ancient Andes: Implications for the Archaeology of Warfare

A review of the evidence for warfare in the prehispanic Andes that challenges the common archaeological idea that many walls and fortresses were symbolic or ritual. It shows that in the period before the Incas, especially from the 12th and 13th centuries, the southern highlands filled with fortified settlements on summits (pucaras), with walls, parapets and slingstones.
It is one of the foundations of the current consensus that warfare between lordships was frequent in the Andes before the Inca expansion, which the Incas presented as a pacification.

fuentes/skeletal-evidence-inca-warfare/t.texto: Skeletal evidence for Inca warfare from the Cuzco region of Peru

fuentes/skeletal-evidence-inca-warfare/a.texto: Valerie A. Andrushko and Elva C. Torres

fuentes/skeletal-evidence-inca-warfare/s.texto: Article (American Journal of Physical Anthropology, vol. 146, no. 3)

fuentes/skeletal-evidence-inca-warfare/r.texto: An analysis of skull injuries in 454 adults from eleven sites in the Cuzco region, from the Middle Horizon, the Wari period (600–1000), to the Inca period. Of them, 22% had some injury, but severe wounds suggesting warfare rose significantly only in the Inca period: 7.8% of adults, compared with 2.5% in the previous period and 2.8% in the Wari period.

fuentes/skeletal-evidence-inca-warfare/p.texto: It adds evidence from bodies to a history of Inca wars based almost only on the chronicles, and shows that in the Cuzco region serious violence increased with the empire, not in the period of the pucaras.

fuentes/ancient-quipu-locke/titulo.texto: The Ancient Quipu or Peruvian Knot Record

fuentes/ancient-quipu-locke/resumen.texto: A study of the quipus in the American Museum of Natural History, in which Locke showed, starting from an earlier 1912 article, that the knots recorded numbers in a positional decimal system and that some cords add up the values of others.

fuentes/ancient-quipu-locke/por_que_impo.texto: It was the first verifiable decipherment of part of the quipu code.

fuentes/ancient-quipu-locke/leer.0.titul.texto: Earlier article by Locke with the same finding (American Anthropologist, 1912), on Internet Archive

fuentes/code-of-the-quipu/titulo.texto: Code of the Quipu: A Study in Media, Mathematics, and Culture

fuentes/code-of-the-quipu/soporte.texto: Book, with Robert Ascher (University of Michigan Press)

fuentes/code-of-the-quipu/resumen.texto: A mathematical analysis of hundreds of quipus that describes their conventions (color, position, knot types, subsidiary cords) and shows that they organized information into categories and hierarchies, in addition to recording numbers.

fuentes/code-of-the-quipu/por_que_import.texto: With its database of quipus, it opened the systematic study of their logic.

fuentes/signs-of-the-inka-khipu/titulo.texto: Signs of the Inka Khipu: Binary Coding in the Andean Knotted-String Records

fuentes/signs-of-the-inka-khipu/resumen.texto: Proposes that quipus were built from a series of binary choices (material, direction of spinning and knotting, color, direction of attachment to the main cord) that formed a code capable of recording more than numbers, perhaps names and narratives.

fuentes/signs-of-the-inka-khipu/por_que_.texto: It is the best-known formulation of the hypothesis that quipus may have functioned as writing, which still has no proven decipherment.

fuentes/khipu-accounting-puruchuco/sopor.texto: Article (Science, vol. 309), with Carrie J. Brezine

fuentes/khipu-accounting-puruchuco/resum.texto: A computer analysis of a group of quipus from Puruchuco, near Lima, showing that they corresponded at three levels: the values of some quipus were added up in others, as in hierarchical administrative accounting. The authors propose that a sequence of cords at the beginning of some quipus identified the place.

fuentes/khipu-accounting-puruchuco/por_q.texto: It is the clearest evidence of the use of quipus at several levels for administration, as the chronicles described.

fuentes/writing-with-twisted-cords/titul.texto: Writing with Twisted Cords: The Inscriptive Capacity of Andean Khipus

fuentes/writing-with-twisted-cords/resum.texto: A study of two quipus kept by the community of San Juan de Collata, in Huarochirí, which its keepers describe as letters from the time of the 18th-century rebellions. Because of the variety of combinations of animal fiber, color and twist, the author proposes that they could record syllables or words, and reads some cords as lineage names.

fuentes/writing-with-twisted-cords/por_q.texto: It is one of the most cited arguments in favor of some quipus having recorded language; the proposal is not confirmed.

fuentes/imperio-socialista-baudin/titulo.texto: The Socialist Empire of the Incas

fuentes/imperio-socialista-baudin/resume.texto: Work by the French liberal economist Louis Baudin describing the Inca state as a planned state socialism imposed from above: land assigned by the state, compulsory labor, storehouses that guaranteed subsistence, and no private ownership of land or markets. Baudin saw in this system material security at the cost of individual freedom.

fuentes/imperio-socialista-baudin/por_qu.texto: Together with Mariátegui’s Seven Essays, published the same year, it fixed the image of an Inca “socialism” or “communism,” admired or criticized from opposite sides; later ethnohistory (Murra, Rostworowski) replaced it with that of an economy of reciprocity and redistribution with a privileged nobility.

fuentes/tihuanacu-posnansky/titulo.texto: Tihuanacu, the Cradle of American Man

fuentes/tihuanacu-posnansky/resumen.texto: Work in which Arthur Posnansky gathered four decades of studies of Tiahuanaco, with plans and photographs of a site that was later greatly altered. He maintains, based on calculations of the astronomical orientation of the Kalasasaya, that the temple was built about 17,000 years ago and that Tiahuanaco was the cradle of American humanity.

fuentes/tihuanacu-posnansky/por_que_impo.texto: His records remain useful; his chronology, refuted by radiocarbon dates that place the peak of Tiahuanaco between 500 and 1000 AD, still circulates in pseudoarchaeological texts.

fuentes/in-the-wonderland-of-peru/resume.texto: A complete issue of the magazine devoted to the 1912 Yale University and National Geographic Society expedition to Machu Picchu, with many photographs. It presented the site to the public as a lost city and proposed, without evidence, that it had been the place of origin of the Incas and the last Inca city of Vilcabamba.

fuentes/in-the-wonderland-of-peru/por_qu.texto: It made Machu Picchu famous worldwide; both identifications were discarded (the Vilcabamba of the last Incas was Espíritu Pampa), and the account of the “discovery” pushed into the background the farmers who lived there and those who had visited it before.

fuentes/misterio-sobre-el-desierto/resum.texto: María Reiche’s first book on the Nazca lines and figures, which she measured and mapped. Following Paul Kosok, she argues that many lines marked the rising and setting of celestial bodies and formed a calendar tied to the agricultural cycle.

fuentes/misterio-sobre-el-desierto/por_q.texto: It spread knowledge of the Nazca lines and helped protect them; the calendar hypothesis was largely discarded by the studies of Gerald Hawkins and Anthony Aveni, who relate the lines to water and ritual paths.

personas/manco-capac/resumen.texto: Legendary founder of the Inca dynasty and of Cuzco. According to Garcilaso, he left Lake Titicaca with his sister and wife Mama Ocllo, sent by the Sun to teach people who, in his account, lived without religion or government, how to live in towns, with laws and agriculture; according to Betanzos, Cieza and Sarmiento, he was one of the four Ayar brothers who came out of the cave of Tambo Toco, in Pacaritambo, and who occupied Cuzco by force, displacing its inhabitants. There is no archaeological evidence of his existence, and the dates given for him are conjectural.

personas/viracocha-inca/resumen.texto: Eighth Inca according to the chronicles, father of Pachacútec. Betanzos and Sarmiento tell that he left Cuzco when the Chancas attacked and took refuge with his heir Inca Urco, and that the defense was led by his son Cusi Yupanqui, who later displaced him; Garcilaso, by contrast, credits him with the victory. Many historians, such as María Rostworowski, explain the differences by the interests of the panacas that informed each chronicler.

personas/huascar/resumen.texto: Son of Huayna Cápac, recognized as Inca in Cuzco after the deaths of his father and of Ninan Cuyochi around 1527. The chronicles describe him at odds with the Cuzco nobility and with the cult of the dead Incas; his war with his half brother Atahualpa ended in his defeat and capture at Quipaipán in 1532. On Atahualpa’s orders, while Atahualpa was already a prisoner of the Spaniards, he was killed on the road to Cajamarca, in late 1532 or early 1533.

personas/ninan-cuyochi/resumen.texto: Son of Huayna Cápac who, according to several chronicles, had been chosen as successor. He died shortly after his father, in the north, in the epidemic that historians usually identify with smallpox, which arrived before the conquistadors; his death left the succession open between Huáscar and Atahualpa.

personas/quisquis/resumen.texto: Atahualpa’s general who, together with Chalcuchímac, defeated Huáscar at Quipaipán in 1532 and occupied Cuzco, where, according to Betanzos, Sarmiento and Garcilaso, he and other envoys of Atahualpa killed the family and supporters of Huáscar. He then fought the Spaniards and their Indigenous allies until 1535, when his own captains killed him.

personas/chalcuchimac/resumen.texto: Atahualpa’s general, victor over Huáscar’s armies in the north and at Quipaipán (1532). In 1533 Hernando Pizarro took him to Cajamarca; accused of directing Indigenous attacks against the Spanish column marching to Cuzco, Francisco Pizarro had him burned alive in the Jaquijahuana Valley, near Cuzco, in November of that year.

personas/cuxirimay-ocllo/resumen.texto: Cuzco noblewoman of the Pachacútec panaca, betrothed or wife of Atahualpa; after his death she was the companion of Francisco Pizarro, with whom she had two children, and later the wife of Juan de Betanzos, under the name Angelina Yupanqui. Historians attribute to information from her lineage that Betanzos’s Suma y narración exalts Pachacútec and presents Atahualpa sympathetically.

personas/jose-de-acosta/resumen.texto: Castilian Jesuit who lived in Peru from 1572 to 1586, was provincial of his order and a theologian at the Third Lima Council, where the trilingual catechism was prepared. He wrote De procuranda indorum salute, on the evangelization of the Indians, and the Natural and Moral History of the Indies (1590), which spread in Europe knowledge of American nature and of the religions and governments of the Incas and Mexica.

personas/bernabe-cobo/resumen.texto: Andalusian Jesuit who arrived in America in 1596 and spent most of his life in Peru, with a period in Mexico (1630–1650). For about forty years he gathered material for his History of the New World, completed in 1653, which describes American nature with a naturalist’s rigor and Inca religion and society based on chronicles, informants and his own observation.

personas/cristobal-de-molina/resumen.texto: Cleric known as “the Cuzco native,” a Quechua preacher at the indigenous hospital of Cuzco and an ecclesiastical visitor. At the request of Bishop Sebastián de Lartaún he wrote around 1575 the Account of the Fables and Rites of the Incas, with informants who had served in the ancient cult. He should not be confused with his contemporary Cristóbal de Molina “the Almagrist.”

personas/martin-de-murua/resumen.texto: Basque Mercedarian friar who served as a parish priest in the southern Andes and wrote two illustrated versions of a history of the Incas (1590 and 1616). Felipe Guaman Poma de Ayala made much of the drawings for the first and later accused him, in his Nueva corónica, of mistreating the Indians of his parish.

personas/blas-valera/resumen.texto: Mestizo Jesuit born in Chachapoyas, son of a conquistador and an Andean woman, who worked as an interpreter and Quechua preacher. He wrote in Latin a history of Peru that was lost; Garcilaso knew it in fragments and cites it often. He is credited with the Account of the Ancient Customs of the Natives of Peru, and the Miccinelli documents attribute to him a life after his official death that most specialists do not accept.

personas/francisco-de-avila/resumen.texto: Cuzco-born cleric, parish priest of San Damián de Checa, in Huarochirí, from 1597. He had the religious traditions of the province gathered into the Quechua Huarochirí manuscript and from 1609 led the campaigns to extirpate idolatry in the archdiocese of Lima, with the destruction of huacas and mummies and public punishments; before that he had been denounced by his parishioners for abuses.

personas/miguel-cabello-balboa/resumen.texto: Andalusian cleric, formerly a soldier, who in Quito wrote the Miscellany of the Antarctic (1586), with a chronology of Inca kings that John Rowe adopted in 1945 and that is still used. He also recorded the legend of Naylamp, from the north coast, and took part in expeditions to the eastern jungle, where he died.

personas/juan-de-velasco/resumen.texto: Jesuit born in Riobamba, expelled with his order in 1767, who wrote in Italy the History of the Kingdom of Quito (1789). His account of the kingdom of the shyris, with no known documentary support, became during the 19th century the basis of Ecuadorian national history before the Incas.

personas/max-uhle/resumen.texto: German archaeologist who worked in Peru, Bolivia, Chile and Ecuador between 1892 and 1933. With Alphons Stübel he published Tiahuanaco (1892), and at Pachacámac (1896) he carried out the first stratigraphic excavation in the Andes, the basis of the cultural sequence still in use. He argued that Andean civilization came from Mesoamerican influences along the coast, an idea that Tello fought.

personas/julio-c-tello/resumen.texto: Physician and archaeologist born in Huarochirí to a Quechua-speaking family, considered the founder of Peruvian archaeology. He studied Chavín de Huántar from 1919, discovered the Paracas cemeteries (1925–1927), and defended the indigenous origin of Andean civilization in the highlands and the Amazon. He founded museums and promoted laws protecting archaeological heritage.

personas/rafael-larco-hoyle/resumen.texto: Peruvian landowner and archaeologist who assembled a large collection of north coast ceramics, the basis of the Larco Museum in Lima. He proposed the first sequence of Moche ceramic styles, defined the Cupisnique culture, and in 1946 proposed a chronology for the north coast.

personas/maria-reiche/resumen.texto: German mathematician who from 1946 measured and mapped the Nazca lines and figures, first under Paul Kosok’s hypothesis that they were an astronomical calendar. Her work and her defense of the pampas contributed to their legal protection and their declaration as a World Heritage Site in 1994.

personas/john-rowe/resumen.texto: American archaeologist, professor at Berkeley, who worked in Cuzco from 1939. In 1945 he proposed the dates of Inca reigns based on Cabello Balboa (Pachacútec from 1438), and in 1946 he published the synthesis of Inca culture in the Handbook of South American Indians; he organized the chronology of horizons and periods of Andean archaeology.

personas/john-murra/resumen.texto: Anthropologist born in Odesa, who fought in the Spanish Civil War and later turned to Inca economics. He used the 16th-century administrative visits of Huánuco and Chucuito to describe reciprocity, state redistribution, and the “vertical control” of ecological zones by Andean groups, and he was one of the founders of Andean ethnohistory.

personas/maria-rostworowski/resumen.texto: Peruvian historian who worked with colonial archival documents (lawsuits, visits, wills) to study the coastal lordships, the curacas, noblewomen and Inca succession. Her History of the Tahuantinsuyu (1988) presented the Incas from an Andean perspective and not only from Cuzco.

personas/tom-zuidema/resumen.texto: Dutch anthropologist who studied the ceque system of Cuzco and proposed a structural reading of Inca history, in which dynastic lists express social organization rather than a linear succession of kings. He taught at the University of Illinois.

personas/luis-lumbreras/resumen.texto: Peruvian archaeologist born in Ayacucho who excavated at Chavín de Huántar and studied the Wari period. Working from a Marxist-inspired social archaeology, he wrote syntheses on the origin of civilization and of the state in the Andes, and directed the National Museum of Anthropology and Archaeology of Peru.

personas/michael-moseley/resumen.texto: American archaeologist at the University of Florida who proposed in 1975 that Andean civilization had maritime bases, in coastal fishing villages that built temples before intensive agriculture. He directed excavations at Chan Chan and studied the effects of earthquakes and El Niño on coastal societies.

personas/christopher-donnan/resumen.texto: American archaeologist specializing in Moche iconography, who identified in ceramic painting the recurring scene of the “sacrifice ceremony,” in which goblets with the blood of prisoners are presented. He collaborated with Walter Alva on the publication of the Sipán tombs.

personas/richard-burger/resumen.texto: American archaeologist, professor at Yale, who excavated at Chavín de Huántar and wrote the standard synthesis on Chavín and the origins of Andean civilization. He directed the radiocarbon dating that in 2021 showed that Machu Picchu had been occupied since around 1420.

personas/ruth-shady/resumen.texto: Peruvian archaeologist who since 1994 has directed research at Caral, in the Supe Valley. Her dates showed that Caral had monumental architecture around 2600 BC, and she maintains that it was the first state-level society in the Americas.

personas/walter-alva/resumen.texto: Peruvian archaeologist who in 1987, after looters opened a tomb at Huaca Rajada, Sipán, excavated with the police and the state the intact tomb of the Lord of Sipán and other elite Moche tombs. He directed the Royal Tombs of Sipán Museum, in Lambayeque.

personas/john-verano/resumen.texto: American bioarchaeologist, professor at Tulane University, who studied the remains of Moche sacrifice victims at the Huaca de la Luna, the child and camelid sacrifices at Huanchaquito-Las Llamas, and skull trepanation in the Andes.

personas/johan-reinhard/resumen.texto: American anthropologist and mountaineer specializing in Inca high-mountain shrines. With Miguel Zárate he found in 1995 the body of the Ampato girl (Juanita), and with Constanza Ceruti, in 1999, the three children of Llullaillaco.

personas/constanza-ceruti/resumen.texto: Argentine archaeologist specializing in Inca high-mountain shrines, who took part in the excavation of the Llullaillaco children (1999) and in many archaeological ascents in the Andes.

personas/gary-urton/resumen.texto: American anthropologist, professor at Harvard, specialist in quipus and Andean astronomy. With Carrie Brezine he founded the Harvard quipu database and proposed that quipus used a binary code capable of recording more than numbers.

personas/sabine-hyland/resumen.texto: American anthropologist, professor at the University of St Andrews, who studies colonial quipus and their relation to language. Her studies of the Collata quipus (2017) fed the hypothesis that some quipus recorded words.

personas/marcia-ascher/resumen.texto: American mathematician who, with anthropologist Robert Ascher, analyzed hundreds of quipus and described their logical conventions; she was one of the founders of ethnomathematics.

personas/arthur-posnansky/resumen.texto: Austrian engineer based in Bolivia who studied Tiahuanaco for four decades. He left valuable plans and photographs, but maintained, through astronomical calculations, that the site was about 17,000 years old, a chronology that radiocarbon dating refuted.

personas/hiram-bingham/resumen.texto: Yale professor who in 1911 reached Machu Picchu guided by local farmers and led expeditions funded by Yale and the National Geographic Society, which took thousands of artifacts to the United States. He later became a senator. Yale returned the artifacts to Peru between 2011 and 2012, after a long claim.

hechos/cultura-valdivia/resumen.texto: Coastal culture of Ecuador, one of the first in the Americas to make pottery, from around 3800 BC, and to live in stable farming villages, with maize, beans, cotton and fishing. It is known for its stone and ceramic female figurines and for villages such as Real Alto, with houses around a plaza. In 1965 Emilio Estrada, Betty Meggers and Clifford Evans proposed that its pottery had been brought by Japanese fishermen of the Jōmon culture; today almost no one accepts that hypothesis, because there is no evidence of contact and the region’s pottery has its own development.

hechos/cultura-chavin/resumen.texto: Religious and artistic tradition centered on the temple of Chavín de Huántar, whose style, with felines, birds of prey, serpents and fanged beings, spread across the highlands and coast of Peru in the first millennium BC, together with weaving, goldworking and ceramic techniques. Julio C. Tello considered it the “mother culture” of Andean civilization; today it is known that it was preceded by monumental centers such as Caral, Sechín and Kotosh, and it is seen more as a great center of worship and pilgrimage than as a state. Richard Burger dates it between 900 and 200 BC, and John Rick proposes that the temple began around 1200 BC.

hechos/cultura-paracas/resumen.texto: Culture of the southern coast of Peru, on the Paracas peninsula and the Ica and Pisco valleys, known for its funerary bundles wrapped in embroidered mantles of wool and cotton, among the finest textiles of the ancient world. Julio C. Tello and Toribio Mejía Xesspe discovered its cemeteries of Cerro Colorado and the necropolis of Wari Kayan, with some 430 bundles, in 1925–1927. They practiced cranial deformation and skull trepanation, often with the patient surviving the operation, and it is considered the forerunner of the Nazca culture.

hechos/cultura-nazca/resumen.texto: Culture of the Nazca and Ica valleys on the southern coast of Peru, known for its polychrome pottery, its underground aqueducts (puquios) and the geoglyphs of the pampas; its ceremonial center was Cahuachi. Hundreds of trophy heads, each with a hole in the forehead for hanging it from a cord and sometimes with the lips sealed with thorns, and their constant presence in ceramics show the importance of warfare and head-taking. It is debated whether they were enemies or ancestors of the community itself; isotope analyses indicate that many were from people of the region.

hechos/cultura-moche/lugar.texto: Huacas del Sol and de la Luna

hechos/cultura-moche/resumen.texto: Society of the north coast of Peru, between the Piura and Huarmey valleys, with large adobe platforms such as the Huacas del Sol and de la Luna, Sipán and El Brujo, and extensive irrigation canals. Its sculpted and painted ceramics realistically depict people, animals, diseases, sex, war and sacrifices, and its metalworkers worked gold, silver and copper with advanced techniques. It is debated whether it formed a single state or several lordships grouped into a northern and a southern region; it declined around 600–800, in a period of El Niño rains and droughts that several archaeologists consider one of the causes.

hechos/sacrificios-moche/lugar.texto: Huacas del Sol and de la Luna

hechos/sacrificios-moche/resumen.texto: Moche painting repeats a scene that Christopher Donnan called the “sacrifice ceremony”: defeated warriors are stripped, bound and beheaded, and high-ranking figures drink their blood from goblets. In plaza 3A of the Huaca de la Luna, Steve Bourget excavated in the 1990s the remains of at least 70 young men with fractures, throat cuts, cut marks and dismemberment, some buried in mud from heavy rains, and John Verano interprets them as sacrificed prisoners of war. It is debated whether the prisoners came from wars between lordships or from ritual combat; the tombs of Sipán and San José de Moro showed that those officiating at the scene were royal officials.

hechos/tumba-del-senor-de-sipan/titulo.texto: Tomb of the Lord of Sipán

hechos/tumba-del-senor-de-sipan/resumen.texto: Intact tomb of a 3rd-century Moche ruler, found in 1987 by Walter Alva at Huaca Rajada, after looters had emptied another tomb at the same site and sold its pieces. The lord was buried with ear spools, necklaces, scepters and weapons of gold, silver and copper, together with three young women, several men, a child, a dog and llamas; his attributes match those of the warrior priest of the “sacrifice ceremony.” His objects are in the Royal Tombs of Sipán Museum, in Lambayeque.

hechos/senora-de-cao/resumen.texto: Mummy of a Moche woman about 20 to 25 years old, with snake and spider tattoos on her arms and legs, found in 2005 in the Huaca Cao Viejo of the El Brujo complex by Régulo Franco’s team. She was buried around the year 450 with weapons, crowns and gold and copper ornaments, and with a teenage girl who, according to the excavators, was strangled to accompany her. Her excavators interpret her as a ruler, the first woman of that rank known among the Moche, which changed the idea that only men exercised power there.

hechos/cultura-recuay/resumen.texto: Culture of the Áncash highlands, in the Callejón de Huaylas, contemporary with the Moche, with fortified villages, underground galleries, elite tombs and stone sculptures of warriors with trophy heads. Its kaolin ceramics show lords surrounded by women and llamas in scenes of banquets and ancestor worship.

hechos/cultura-lima/resumen.texto: Culture of the Rímac, Chillón and Lurín valleys on the central coast of Peru, which built adobe pyramids such as Huaca Pucllana and the first temples of Pachacámac, and expanded the irrigation canals that the city of Lima continued to use. At Huaca Pucllana, burials of young women were found that archaeologists interpret as sacrifices.

hechos/cultura-pucara/resumen.texto: The first great complex society of the northern Titicaca basin, centered at Pucará, in Puno: stone temples with sunken courts, sculptures of felines and of figures with trophy heads, and pottery that anticipates Tiahuanaco motifs. It declined in the first centuries of our era, when Tiahuanaco grew to the south of the lake.

hechos/cultura-tiwanaku/resumen.texto: Society that between roughly 500 and 1100 had its capital at Tiahuanaco, south of Titicaca, at 3,800 meters above sea level, and extended its influence over the altiplano, northern Chile and the Moquegua and Cochabamba valleys, with colonies and llama caravans. It farmed raised fields (suka kollus), and its art, such as the Gate of the Sun, shares with Huari the figure of the staff-bearing god. In the Akapana pyramid, dismembered human remains were found that are interpreted as sacrifices. Its fall is attributed to a prolonged drought (Alan Kolata) or to internal conflicts; afterwards the Aymara lordships of the Colla, the Lupaca and others emerged around the lake.

hechos/imperio-wari/resumen.texto: State with its capital at Huari, near Ayacucho, which between about 600 and 1000 built centers of orthogonal architecture across much of the highlands and coast of Peru, such as Pikillacta, next to Cuzco, and Viracochapampa, in the north, linked by roads that the Incas later used. Many archaeologists consider it the first Andean empire and a precedent for Inca administration, with quipus, storehouses and rotating labor; others see a less centralized network. Trophy heads and the injuries from Conchopata and other sites show that its expansion included war and the capture of enemies, and in 2013 an intact mausoleum of Wari elite women was found at El Castillo de Huarmey.

hechos/cultura-sican/resumen.texto: Culture of the north coast of Peru centered at Batán Grande, in the Lambayeque valley, known for its gold and arsenical copper metallurgy and its funerary masks. The elite tombs excavated by Izumi Shimada contain lords buried with large quantities of metal and with women who, according to the excavators, were sacrificed to accompany them. The legend of Naylamp, recorded by Cabello Balboa, tells of the arrival by sea of a dynasty’s founder; the lordship was conquered by the Chimú around 1375.

hechos/cultura-chimu/resumen.texto: Kingdom of the north coast of Peru with its capital at Chan Chan, next to present-day Trujillo, which at its greatest extent dominated the coast from Tumbes to the Chillón valley, near Lima, with large irrigation works and highly developed goldwork. Its kings lived in large walled enclosures where they were buried with offerings and, according to the excavators, with dozens of sacrificed young women. The Incas conquered it around 1470, took its king Minchancaman to Cuzco and moved its goldsmiths to work for the state.

hechos/sacrificio-de-huanchaquito-las-ll.texto: Mass Sacrifice of Children and Llamas at Huanchaquito-Las Llamas

At a coastal site near Chan Chan, Gabriel Prieto and John Verano excavated between 2011 and 2016 the remains of 137 children and adolescents aged 5 to 14, three adults and about 200 young camelids, buried in a single episode around 1450, in the time of the Chimú kingdom. The children have cuts on the sternum and separated ribs, a sign that their chests were opened, perhaps to remove the heart, and footprints in the mud show a procession after heavy rains; the authors propose linking the sacrifice to an El Niño episode. According to its authors, it is the largest known mass sacrifice of children in the Americas, and isotopes and cranial deformation suggest that the victims came from different regions.

hechos/cultura-chachapoyas/resumen.texto: Peoples of the cloud forests of northeastern Peru, between the Marañón and Huallaga rivers, known for their settlements of circular stone houses such as Kuélap, their clay sarcophagi on cliffs and their mausoleums with mummies. They did not form a unified state but lordships that were often at odds with one another. The Incas conquered them around 1470 and, after several rebellions, deported many as mitimaes, so that many Chachapoyas allied with the Spaniards after 1532.

hechos/senorio-de-chincha/resumen.texto: Lordship of the southern coast of Peru, in the Chincha valley, with its center at La Centinela. According to an anonymous report from around 1570, it had thousands of merchants who traded by sea and by land with Quito, Cuzco and the Collao, among other things in Spondylus shells from the coast of Ecuador, and María Rostworowski interpreted it as a lordship of merchants. It was incorporated into the Tawantinsuyu around 1470–1480, under conditions that the chronicles describe differently, and its lord had a privileged place at court: according to Pedro Pizarro, he was the only lord, besides Atahualpa, who arrived in a litter at the plaza of Cajamarca, where he died in November 1532.

hechos/pueblo-chanca/resumen.texto: Peoples of the Andahuaylas region, in present-day Apurímac, whom the chronicles present as a powerful warrior confederation that attacked Cuzco at the start of the 15th century and was defeated by Pachacútec. The archaeological survey by Brian Bauer and his team (2010) found for that period fortified villages on summits and no major political center, which suggests scattered groups at odds with one another rather than a state. After the Inca conquest its region received administrative centers and mitimaes.

hechos/reino-lupaca/resumen.texto: Aymara-speaking lordship on the southwestern shore of Lake Titicaca, with its capital at Chucuito and seven head settlements, governed by two lords, one for each moiety (Cari and Cusi in the 16th century). According to Cieza, its lord Cari fought the Colla of Hatuncolla and allied with the Incas before being incorporated into the Tawantinsuyu. The 1567 visit shows large herds of llamas and alpacas and colonies on the Pacific coast and in the eastern valleys, the case John Murra used for his model of the “vertical archipelago.”

hechos/pueblo-canari/resumen.texto: People of the southern highlands of present-day Ecuador, in the provinces of Cañar and Azuay, organized in lordships. They resisted the conquest of Topa Inca and were subjugated; the Incas built the city of Tomebamba on top of their center at Guapondélig and moved many Cañari as mitimaes and guards to Cuzco and other regions. During the civil war they supported Huáscar, and Atahualpa punished them with the massacres recorded by Cieza de León; afterwards they allied with the Spaniards.

hechos/caranquis-y-cayambes/resumen.texto: Lordships of the northern highlands of present-day Ecuador, between Quito and the present border with Colombia, which raised earthen mounds (tolas) and fortresses. They were among the last peoples incorporated into the Tawantinsuyu: according to the chronicles they resisted Huayna Cápac for years from the pucarás of Pambamarca and others, until the massacre of Yahuarcocha. Unlike the “kingdom of Quito” of the shyris described by Juan de Velasco, these lordships are documented in chronicles, visits and excavations.

hechos/pueblo-huanca/resumen.texto: People of the Mantaro valley, in the central highlands of Peru. Between about 1350 and 1460 they lived in large walled towns on the summits, such as Tunanmarca and Hatunmarca, a sign of wars between their divisions, according to the excavations of Timothy Earle, Terence D’Altroy and their team. The Incas conquered them, brought them down to the valleys and built the administrative center of Hatun Xauxa; in 1533 the Huanca allied with the Spaniards and later presented accounts in quipus of what they had handed over.

hechos/cultura-mantena/resumen.texto: Culture of the coast of Ecuador, in the present-day provinces of Manabí, Santa Elena and Guayas, of merchants and navigators who used large log rafts with sails to carry Spondylus shells, textiles and metals along the Pacific coast. In 1526 the expedition of Bartolomé Ruiz found one of these rafts loaded with goods on the open sea, one of the first contacts of the Spaniards with the Andean world. They are also known for their U-shaped stone seats.

hechos/pucaras-antes-de-los-incas/titulo.texto: Warfare and Pucarás before the Incas

hechos/pucaras-antes-de-los-incas/resume.texto: After the fall of Huari and Tiahuanaco, between the 12th and 15th centuries, much of the highlands filled with walled towns on summits (pucaras), with walls, ditches, parapets and stockpiles of slingstones, especially in the Titicaca basin, the Mantaro valley and Andahuaylas. The studies of Elizabeth Arkush and Charles Stanish on these fortified towns indicate frequent wars between lordships, although in the Cuzco region severe skull injuries increased only in Inca times (Andrushko and Torres, 2011). The chronicles remember that period as the time of the sinchis, warrior chiefs, and the Incas presented their conquest as the end of that disorder.

hechos/mito-de-origen-de-los-incas/resum.texto: The chronicles record two main accounts: that of Manco Cápac and Mama Ocllo, children of the Sun who came out of Lake Titicaca to teach the peoples, which Garcilaso spread, and that of the four Ayar brothers and their wives who came out of the cave of Tambo Toco, in Pacaritambo, recorded by Betanzos, Cieza and Sarmiento, in which several brothers turn into sacred stones and Manco’s group occupies Cuzco, expelling or forcibly subjugating its inhabitants. Sarmiento, who was writing at the request of Viceroy Toledo, stresses that violence to present the Incas as usurpers; Garcilaso, who also mentions the fable of the brothers, favors the Titicaca version and presents the Incas as bearers of laws and order.

hechos/guerra-contra-los-chancas/titulo.texto: War between Cusco and the Chanca

hechos/guerra-contra-los-chancas/resumen.texto: According to Betanzos and Sarmiento, with variants in Cieza, the Chanca attacked Cusco. Viracocha Inca and his heir Inca Urco abandoned the city, and another son, Cusi Yupanqui, organized its defense, helped according to the account by stones that turned into warriors (the pururaucas). After winning, he took the name Pachacútec and power. Garcilaso attributes the victory to Viracocha Inca. The date of 1438 comes from the chronology of Cabello Balboa adopted by Rowe; archaeology in Andahuaylas has found no Chanca state, and many historians read the episode as a narrative that legitimized Pachacútec against the displaced heir.

hechos/tawantinsuyu/resumen.texto: The Inca state, called Tawantinsuyu in Quechua, “the four parts together”: Chinchaysuyu to the northwest, Antisuyu to the northeast, Collasuyu to the southeast and Contisuyu to the southwest, centered on Cusco. In less than a century it spread from southern present-day Colombia to central Chile and northwestern Argentina, over 4,000 kilometers, through war and through pacts with local lords. It was organized without money or an official market, with tribute in labor (mit'a), storehouses, the royal road, quipus and Quechua as the general language. Estimates of its population around 1525 range from about 6 million (John Rowe, 1946) to about 9 million for present-day Peru alone (Noble David Cook, 1981), and Henry Dobyns proposed more than 30 million. The dates of its expansion, based on the chronology of Cabello Balboa, are under review.

hechos/reconstruccion-del-cusco/resumen.texto: According to Betanzos and Sarmiento, Pachacútec rebuilt the city after the war with the Chanca. He channeled the Saphy and Tullumayo rivers, laid out the great plazas of Haucaypata and Cusipata, built palaces for the royal lineages, rebuilt the Coricancha and relocated other residents to the surrounding area. Betanzos says he called the city “body of a lion,” which led to the idea, popularized by John Rowe, that its plan was shaped like a puma, with Sacsayhuamán as its head. Other authors read this as a metaphor. The city was divided into two halves, Hanan and Hurin, and was organized into ceques radiating from the Coricancha.

hechos/conquista-del-collao/titulo.texto: Inca conquest of the Collao and the Colla rebellion

hechos/conquista-del-collao/resumen.texto: According to Cieza and Sarmiento, the Incas subjugated the Colla of Hatuncolla, who were at war with the Lupaca of Chucuito, during the reigns of Viracocha Inca and Pachacútec. Later the Colla rebelled, according to Sarmiento taking advantage of a rumor that Topa Inca had died on a campaign in the jungle. The Inca suppressed them in a long campaign in which their fortresses were taken and their leaders executed. The Titicaca region later became a center of Inca worship, with the shrine of the Island of the Sun.

hechos/conquista-inca-del-chimor/titulo.texto: Inca conquest of the Chimú kingdom

hechos/conquista-inca-del-chimor/resumen.texto: According to the chronicles, an Inca army led by Cápac Yupanqui and Topa Inca defeated Minchancaman, lord of Chimor, who was taken to Cusco, while a successor of his remained as a subordinate lord. The Incas carried off the treasure of Chan Chan and relocated many Chimú goldsmiths and artisans to Cusco to work for the state. The north coast was left divided into smaller lordships.

hechos/conquista-inca-de-los-chachapoyas.texto: Inca conquest of the Chachapoya and their rebellions

According to the chronicles, Topa Inca conquered the Chachapoya after fierce resistance, and they rebelled more than once. Huayna Cápac put down a rebellion, punished its leaders and relocated many Chachapoya as mitimaes to other regions, including Cusco and Quito. Garcilaso, by contrast, says the Inca pardoned them at the plea of a woman from the region. The resistance and the deportations explain why many Chachapoya sided with the Spanish after 1532.

hechos/conquista-inca-del-norte/titulo.texto: Inca conquest of the Cañari and the Quito highlands

hechos/conquista-inca-del-norte/resumen.texto: According to the chronicles, Topa Inca conquered the Cañari and the peoples of the highlands as far as Quito, first as a general for his father, and founded Tomebamba as the center of the north. Huayna Cápac, who according to tradition was born in Tomebamba, completed the conquest of the northern highlands against the Caranqui, Cayambe and Pasto in wars that lasted years, and spent much of his reign there. The north became the base of the empire’s most experienced army, which later supported Atahualpa.

hechos/matanza-de-yahuarcocha/resumen.texto: According to Cabello Balboa, Sarmiento, Cieza and other chroniclers, after years of resistance by the Caranqui and Cayambe, Huayna Cápac’s army took their fortresses and killed large numbers of the defeated on the shore of a lagoon near present-day Ibarra, which for that reason was called Yahuarcocha, “lake of blood.” The chronicles give death tolls ranging from thousands to tens of thousands that cannot be verified, and the date, between 1495 and 1520 depending on the author, is uncertain. It was the last major Inca conquest campaign in the north.

hechos/ejercito-y-guerra-inca/titulo.texto: Army and warfare in the Tawantinsuyu

hechos/ejercito-y-guerra-inca/resumen.texto: The Inca army was formed from men of the communities who served in turns as part of the mit'a, under noble commanders, and was supplied from the storehouses along the road. It used slings, maces with stone or bronze heads, bolas and lances. The chronicles say the Incas first offered submission with gifts, and punished resistance and rebellion harshly, with executions of leaders, deportations, and trophies such as drums made from enemies’ skin or cups made from their skulls. In the Cusco region, severe skull injuries suggesting warfare increased significantly during the Inca period, according to a study by Valerie Andrushko and Elva Torres (2011).

hechos/represion-de-los-canaris/resumen.texto: During the civil war the Cañari supported Huáscar. According to Cieza de León, who traveled the region in the 1540s, Atahualpa took Tomebamba, destroyed it and killed many Cañari, and in his time the province had many more women than men because of that slaughter. The punishment explains why the Cañari allied with the Spanish and served during the colonial period as guards and auxiliaries in Cusco.

hechos/mita-inca/resumen.texto: A labor tribute in rotating turns that each community owed the Inca state. Married men, organized by their curacas, worked the lands of the Inca and the Sun, served in the army, built roads, bridges and buildings, worked in the mines and carried loads, and the state provided them food and chicha during their service. Inspections of Huánuco and Chucuito show that each group met fixed quotas according to its population. The Spanish took the name and the idea for the colonial mita, with different purposes and different conditions.

hechos/mitmaq/titulo.texto: Mitimaes: population transfers in the Tawantinsuyu

hechos/mitmaq/resumen.texto: The Incas moved entire groups of families, called mitmaqkuna or mitimaes, from their homeland to other regions: loyal peoples to newly conquered areas to watch over them and spread Quechua, rebellious peoples to distant lands to break their resistance, and colonists to farm state lands, guard frontiers or work as artisans. Cieza describes the system as a policy of security and integration. Many historians today describe it as forced deportation on a large scale. The mitimaes kept their clothing and their original headdresses, and the mixing of groups that resulted can still be seen in colonial censuses.

hechos/mitimaes-de-cochabamba/titulo.texto: State colonization of the Cochabamba valley

hechos/mitimaes-de-cochabamba/resumen.texto: According to 16th-century judicial documents, Huayna Cápac removed much of the original population from much of the Cochabamba valley and brought thousands of workers from different peoples of the Collasuyu, many in rotating turns, to grow maize on state lands. The harvest was stored in about 2,400 storehouses at Cotapachi and sent to Cusco and the armies. Nathan Wachtel studied the case as an example of the scale of Inca planning and of forced relocation.

hechos/yanaconas-del-inca/resumen.texto: Servants taken from their communities to work permanently for the Inca, the noble lineages, the temples or the curacas, without the rotation of the mit'a. The status was hereditary. Sarmiento attributes their origin to rebels pardoned by Topa Inca. There was no market in people, but many authors compare their condition to serfdom or slavery, and others note that some yanaconas reached positions of trust. After 1532 many entered the service of the Spanish, and from this comes the colonial yanaconazgo.

hechos/acllas/resumen.texto: Girls chosen by Inca officials in all the provinces and secluded in special houses (acllawasi) in Cusco and in provincial centers, where they wove fine cloth (cumbi) and prepared chicha for worship and redistribution. Some were dedicated to the Sun, others were given by the Inca as wives to nobles, warriors or allied lords, and some were sacrificed in the capacocha. The Spanish called them “virgins of the Sun” and compared them to nuns, a comparison that historians qualify.

hechos/ayllu/resumen.texto: The basic social unit of the Andes: a group of families related, real or symbolic, who recognized a common ancestor, held land and pastures in common, and helped one another through reciprocal labor (ayni, minca). Several ayllus formed larger units, divided into two moieties and governed by curacas. The Inca state organized its tribute on this basis, and the ayllu survived colonial rule and the republics in communities in Peru and Bolivia.

hechos/curacas/resumen.texto: Ethnic lords of the Andean ayllus and lordships, who organized labor, distributed land and redistributed goods in exchange for services from their subjects. The Inca kept them as intermediaries, gave them gifts, women and textiles, and required them to send their sons to Cusco, where they stayed as guarantees and learned Inca customs. Those who rebelled were replaced or executed. Under Spanish rule they continued as caciques, intermediaries for tribute and the mita.

hechos/panacas-y-mallquis/titulo.texto: The panacas and the cult of the dead Incas

hechos/panacas-y-mallquis/resumen.texto: Each dead Inca was mummified (mallqui) and continued to be treated as living by his panaca, the lineage of his descendants, which kept his lands, servants and property, took him out during festivals and spoke on his behalf. In 1984 Geoffrey Conrad and Arthur Demarest proposed that this divided inheritance pushed each new Inca to conquer lands of his own. According to Pedro Pizarro, Huáscar even said that the dead should be buried and stripped of their possessions. Disputes between panacas shaped the versions of Inca history recorded by the chroniclers.

hechos/quipu/resumen.texto: Cords of cotton or wool with knots, which the quipucamayos used to record censuses, tribute and storehouse contents and, according to the chronicles, also genealogies and narratives. They are known from the Wari period. About a thousand survive, nearly all without an exact provenance. In 1912 Leland Locke showed that they recorded numbers in a decimal system. In the early colonial years Spanish courts accepted quipu accounts as evidence, the Third Council of Lima ordered the destruction of those used in rites considered idolatrous, and in some villages they continued to be used into the 20th century.

hechos/debate-sobre-la-escritura-de-los-.texto: Debate over whether the quipus recorded language

Several chronicles state that the quipucamayos “read” histories and laws from the quipus, while Garcilaso maintains that they recorded numbers and served only as a memory aid. Since the studies of Marcia and Robert Ascher (1981) and Gary Urton (2003), it has been debated whether some quipus encoded words, such as names of people and places, and not only numbers. In 2017 Sabine Hyland proposed a partial reading of two colonial quipus from Collata. The quipu database that Urton founded at Harvard with Carrie Brezine has allowed comparison of hundreds of examples. To date, no proposal has achieved a verified decipherment.

hechos/qhapaq-nan/resumen.texto: A network of roads of about 30,000 to 40,000 kilometers that linked Cusco with all the provinces, with two main axes, one through the highlands and one along the coast, and that partly used older roads. It had suspension bridges of plant fiber, stairways and causeways, and every few leagues there were tambos with storehouses and lodging. The chasquis, messengers who relayed from post to post, ran along it. Its use was reserved for officials, armies and those performing service. Cieza compared it to Roman roads, and in 2014 UNESCO declared the network, spanning six countries, a World Heritage Site.

hechos/tambos-y-colcas/titulo.texto: Tambos and storehouses (colcas) of the Inca state

hechos/tambos-y-colcas/resumen.texto: The Incas built thousands of storehouses (colcas) along the road, in rows on the slopes to take advantage of cold and wind, where they kept maize, dried potatoes, charqui, textiles, weapons and tools for the army, for workers on rotation and for festivals. There are groups of hundreds of colcas at Huánuco Pampa and Hatun Xauxa, and about 2,400 at Cotapachi, in Cochabamba. The conquistadors left testimony of their astonishment at these full storehouses in 1532–1533, and of their emptying in the following years.

hechos/capacocha/resumen.texto: A state Inca ceremony in which boys and girls from the provinces, chosen for their physical perfection, were brought to Cusco. From there, after rites and symbolic marriages, they were led in procession to huacas and mountain peaks across the empire and sacrificed with offerings, on occasions such as the coronation or death of an Inca, epidemics or droughts. Betanzos, Molina and Cobo describe it, and in 1621 Rodrigo Hernández Príncipe recorded the case of Tanta Carhua, daughter of a curaca of Ocros, whose sacrifice brought prestige to her family. Archaeology has confirmed the rite with the children of Ampato, Llullaillaco, Aconcagua and El Plomo, among others. The Jesuit Anonymous and Garcilaso denied or minimized Inca human sacrifice.

hechos/capacocha-del-ampato/resumen.texto: The frozen body of a girl aged 12 to 15, sacrificed by the Incas on the summit of Ampato volcano, in Arequipa, around 1440–1480. It was found in 1995 by Johan Reinhard and Miguel Zárate, after ash from a neighboring volcano melted the ice at the summit and the bundle rolled down the slope. Studies showed that she died from a blow to the head and had eaten vegetables hours before. She is displayed at the Museo Santuarios Andinos in Arequipa.

hechos/capacocha-del-aconcagua/resumen.texto: The body of a boy about 7 years old, sacrificed in a capacocha around the year 1500 on Cerro Pirámide, in the Aconcagua massif, at about 5,300 meters. Mountaineers found him in 1985, and archaeologist Juan Schobinger studied him. A DNA analysis published in 2015 identified a maternal lineage that is very rare today.

hechos/nino-del-cerro-el-plomo/titulo.texto: The boy of Cerro El Plomo
