hechos/nino-del-cerro-el-plomo/resumen.texto: The frozen body of a boy about 8 or 9 years old, sacrificed by the Incas on Cerro El Plomo, near Santiago, Chile, at more than 5,000 meters. Muleteers searching for treasure found him in 1954, and the National Museum of Natural History of Chile purchased him. He was one of the first capacocha bodies studied, and evidence that the Inca cult reached the Mapocho valley.

hechos/sistema-de-ceques/resumen.texto: According to the list preserved by Cobo, 41 imaginary lines (ceques) radiated from the Coricancha toward the horizon and ordered about 328 huacas of the Cusco valley: springs, stones, hills, tombs and places of memorable events. Each was looked after by a group from the city, which made offerings there on fixed dates. R. Tom Zuidema interpreted it as a system uniting kinship, calendar, irrigation and hierarchy. In the 1990s Brian Bauer located many of these huacas on the ground.

hechos/huacas-y-oraculos/resumen.texto: In the Andes, huaca meant anything sacred: mountains, stones, springs, mummies of ancestors, temples and images. Some had famous oracles, such as Pachacámac on the central coast or Catequil in Huamachuco, which pilgrims visited with offerings. They formed kinship groups and alliances like those described in the Huarochirí manuscript. The Incas incorporated the huacas of conquered peoples into their worship and took some to Cusco as hostages. According to the chronicles, Atahualpa ordered the destruction of the Catequil huaca for having predicted his defeat.

hechos/epidemia-andina-de-1525/titulo.texto: Epidemic and the death of Huayna Cápac

hechos/epidemia-andina-de-1525/resumen.texto: Around 1525–1528, before the Spanish had entered the Tawantinsuyu, an epidemic killed Huayna Cápac in the north, his heir Ninan Cuyochi and, according to the chronicles, many nobles and commoners. Most historians identify it as smallpox, which arrived from Panama or the Caribbean through Indigenous exchange, although others propose measles or another disease, and the descriptions do not allow confirmation. The deaths of the Inca and his heir opened the civil war.

hechos/guerra-civil-inca/titulo.texto: Civil war between Huáscar and Atahualpa

hechos/guerra-civil-inca/resumen.texto: After the death of Huayna Cápac and his heir, Huáscar was recognized as Inca in Cusco, while his half brother Atahualpa remained in the north with the veteran army and his generals Quisquis, Chalcuchímac and Rumiñahui. Around 1529 the war began. Huáscar’s army, led by Atoc, was defeated in the north. Atahualpa punished the Cañari who had supported his brother, and his generals advanced south until they defeated and captured Huáscar at Quipaipán in 1532. The chronicles differ according to the side of their informants. Betanzos, married to a woman of Pachacútec’s panaca, sympathizes with Atahualpa. Garcilaso, whose mother belonged to Topa Inca’s panaca, which Atahualpa’s generals decimated, presents him as a tyrant. The war left the empire divided when the Spanish arrived.

hechos/batalla-de-quipaipan/resumen.texto: The decisive battle of the Inca civil war, fought in 1532 near Cusco, in which Atahualpa’s generals Quisquis and Chalcuchímac defeated Huáscar’s army and captured him. Atahualpa received the news in the northern highlands, shortly before his meeting with Pizarro at Cajamarca.

hechos/matanza-de-los-partidarios-de-hua.texto: Massacre of Huáscar’s family and supporters in Cusco

According to Betanzos, Sarmiento and Garcilaso, after Quipaipán, Atahualpa’s envoys, among them Cusi Yupanqui, and the general Quisquis killed Huáscar’s wives, children and relatives in Cusco, along with nobles of his faction, especially from Topa Inca’s panaca. They also burned that Inca’s mummy. Garcilaso, a descendant of those harmed, gives the cruelest details. Betanzos, informed by Atahualpa’s side, also recounts it. The massacre decimated the Cusco nobility shortly before the Spanish conquest.

hechos/hallazgo-de-las-momias-de-los-inc.texto: Polo de Ondegardo confiscates the Inca mummies

In 1559 the corregidor of Cusco, Juan Polo de Ondegardo, searched for and confiscated the mummies of several Incas, among them those of Pachacútec and Huayna Cápac, and of some coyas, which their panacas were still venerating in secret, along with huacas and cult objects. Several were taken to Lima and kept in the hospital of San Andrés. Garcilaso saw some in Cusco before their transfer, and José de Acosta describes Pachacútec’s. Their whereabouts were lost, and archaeological searches in the former hospital did not find them.

hechos/polemica-sobre-la-tirania-inca/ti.texto: Controversy over the legitimacy of the Incas

hechos/polemica-sobre-la-tirania-inca/re.texto: Between 1570 and 1572 Viceroy Francisco de Toledo had testimony taken from Andean elders (the Informaciones) and commissioned Pedro Sarmiento de Gamboa to write a history to prove that the Incas were recent conquerors who had usurped power from the natural lords. This would make the King of Spain their legitimate successor and undermine the Las Casas claim to return government to them. In response, authors such as Blas Valera and the Inca Garcilaso (1609) presented the Incas as nearly monotheistic and benevolent rulers who had lifted peoples living without laws out of a life that, according to Garcilaso, included human sacrifice and cannibalism. They denied or minimized the human sacrifices of the Incas themselves. Both images served political interests. Archaeology shows that the Incas succeeded complex societies such as Huari, Tiahuanaco and Chimú, and that their expansion combined war and negotiation.

hechos/debate-sobre-la-cronologia-inca/r.texto: The most frequently cited dates of Inca history (Pachacútec from 1438, Topa Inca from 1471, Huayna Cápac from 1493) come from the Miscelánea antártica of Cabello Balboa, adopted by John Rowe in 1945; no other chronicle confirms them. Radiocarbon dates from Inca sites in Cusco, at Machu Picchu (occupied from around 1420 according to Richard Burger and others, 2021), in northwestern Argentina and in Chile suggest that the expansion began decades earlier. Other authors, such as Zuidema, even doubt that the list of kings is a historical succession.

hechos/tesis-del-socialismo-inca/resumen.texto: In 1928 the liberal economist Louis Baudin described the Inca state as a state socialism that gave material security in exchange for freedom. José Carlos Mariátegui, in his Siete ensayos, spoke of an Inca “agrarian communism” whose base, the ayllu, could sustain a Peruvian socialism. The image, taken up by both critics and admirers of socialism, rested mainly on Garcilaso’s descriptions. Later ethnohistory, with Murra and Rostworowski, instead describes an economy of reciprocity and redistribution, with a nobility living off the compulsory labor of the communities, and considers these labels anachronistic.

hechos/documentos-miccinelli/resumen.texto: Manuscripts from a private collection in Naples, made known from 1996 by Laura Laurencich Minelli. According to them, Blas Valera did not die in 1597 but secretly returned to Peru, wrote with other Jesuits the Nueva corónica attributed to Guaman Poma, and recorded that the quipus had a syllabic script. They also include an alleged letter from the conquistador Francisco de Chaves about the poisoning of Atahualpa’s captains at Cajamarca. Most specialists, such as Rolena Adorno and Juan Carlos Estenssoro, consider them forgeries or, at least, unproven documents, because of their anachronisms and the restricted access to the originals. Their defenders maintain that they are authentic.

hechos/mito-del-reino-de-quito/titulo.texto: The “kingdom of Quito” of the Shyris

hechos/mito-del-reino-de-quito/resumen.texto: According to Juan de Velasco’s Historia del reino de Quito (1789), the caras or shyris, who arrived by sea on the coast of Ecuador, conquered the Quito highlands around the year 1000 and formed a kingdom that lasted until the Inca conquest. Velasco says he used lost writings, and there is no other colonial document or archaeological evidence of this kingdom. Since Jacinto Jijón y Caamaño, most historians consider it an 18th-century construction, although it became the basis of Ecuador’s national history and continued to be taught. The regional lordships, such as the Caranqui, Cayambe, Puruhá and Cañari, are documented.

hechos/seudoarqueologia-andina/resumen.texto: Some Andean sites are the subject of theories with no scientific basis: the 17,000-year age that Arthur Posnansky attributed to Tiahuanaco; Erich von Däniken’s idea (1968) that the Nazca lines were runways or signals for extraterrestrial visitors; and the so-called “Nazca mummies” of nonhuman beings, presented from 2017 and brought to the Congress of Mexico in 2023, which according to Peruvian experts were dolls assembled from human and animal bones. Critics point out that these theories deny Andean peoples authorship of their own works.

hechos/expedicion-de-bingham-a-machu-pic.texto: On July 24, 1911, Hiram Bingham, a Yale professor, arrived at Machu Picchu guided by the farmer Melchor Arteaga and found families there who farmed the terraces. Others had visited before, such as Agustín Lizárraga, who left his name on a wall in 1902, and the site appeared on 19th-century maps. The expeditions of 1912 and 1915 cleared the site, and thousands of objects were taken to Yale under temporary permits from the Peruvian government, which Yale returned only between 2011 and 2012. Bingham presented it to the world as a “lost city” and misidentified it with Vilcabamba.

hechos/saqueo-de-huacas/lugar.texto: Huacas del Sol and de la Luna

hechos/saqueo-de-huacas/resumen.texto: From the conquest on, the Spanish looked for gold and silver in temples and tombs. In 1533 the pieces of the Coricancha and Pachacámac were melted down for Atahualpa’s ransom. At the beginning of the 17th century treasure hunters diverted the Moche River to undermine the Huaca del Sol, which lost much of its structure. Colonial authorities treated these excavations as mining and collected the royal fifth on what was found. Looting to sell pieces continued into the republic: in the 20th century thousands of tombs were emptied at Batán Grande and other sites, and in 1987 the looting of a tomb at Sipán led to the discovery of the Lord of Sipán’s tomb.

hechos/trepanacion-andina/resumen.texto: From the Paracas culture, around the 4th century BC, to the Incas, Andean surgeons opened the skull by scraping, cutting or boring the bone, mainly to treat fractures and other injuries. John Verano studied more than 800 trepanned skulls and found that the proportion of patients who survived, visible in the regenerated bone, increased over time to more than three quarters in Inca times. Julio C. Tello and other Peruvian physicians studied it from the early 20th century.

lugares/real-alto/resumen.texto: A village of the Valdivia culture on the Santa Elena peninsula, on the coast of Ecuador, one of the first farming villages in South America, with oval houses around a plaza and ceremonial mounds. It was excavated by Donald Lathrap and Jorge Marcos in the 1970s.

lugares/kotosh/resumen.texto: A site near Huánuco with superimposed temples from the Late Archaic, including the Temple of the Crossed Hands, with a clay relief of two forearms crossed and chambers with ritual hearths. A mission from the University of Tokyo excavated it from 1960, and it gave its name to a religious tradition of the highlands that predates Chavín.

lugares/cerro-sechin/resumen.texto: A temple in the Casma valley, on the north coast of Peru, surrounded by a wall of about 300 carved monoliths showing armed warriors and mutilated victims: split bodies, severed heads, viscera and eyes. Julio C. Tello excavated it in 1937. It is debated whether it represents a military victory, a sacrificial rite or a myth, but it is one of the oldest images of organized violence in the Americas.

lugares/chavin-de-huantar/resumen.texto: A ceremonial center in the Áncash highlands, at the confluence of the Mosna and Huachecsa rivers, with a stone temple traversed by underground galleries where the Lanzón, a monolith of a deity with fangs, is preserved. The clavate heads in its walls and the images of beings that transform suggest ritual use of plants such as the San Pedro cactus. Julio C. Tello studied it from 1919. John Rick dates it between 1200 and 500 BC, and Richard Burger to 200 BC. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1985.

lugares/cahuachi/resumen.texto: A ceremonial center of the Nazca culture, with dozens of adobe mounds on natural hills, which functioned as a place of pilgrimage and offerings more than as a city. Giuseppe Orefici excavated it for decades.

lugares/lineas-de-nazca/resumen.texto: Thousands of lines, geometric figures, and figures of animals and plants (the monkey, the hummingbird, the spider) made in the pampas between Nazca and Palpa by removing the reddish stones from the surface, by the Paracas and Nazca cultures. María Reiche measured them for half a century. Today they are linked to water, fertility and ritual paths, and since 2019 hundreds of new figures have been discovered with the help of high-resolution imagery. They have been a World Heritage Site since 1994.

lugares/huaca-rajada/resumen.texto: A Moche funerary platform near Chiclayo, in the Lambayeque valley, where Walter Alva has excavated since 1987 the tomb of the Lord of Sipán and other elite tombs, after the looting of one of them.

lugares/huacas-del-sol-y-de-la-luna/nomb.texto: Huacas del Sol and de la Luna

lugares/huacas-del-sol-y-de-la-luna/resu.texto: A Moche center in the Moche valley, near Trujillo, with the Huaca del Sol, the largest adobe structure in the Americas, and the Huaca de la Luna, a temple with polychrome reliefs of the mountain deity and of warriors and prisoners. Between the two was an urban neighborhood of artisans. In Plaza 3A of the Huaca de la Luna, the remains of more than 70 sacrifice victims were found. Treasure hunters diverted the Moche River in the colonial period to undermine the Huaca del Sol, which lost much of its structure.

lugares/el-brujo/resumen.texto: A complex in the Chicama valley, on the north coast of Peru, with the Huaca Cao Viejo, a Moche temple where the tomb of the Lady of Cao was found in 2005, and the Huaca Prieta, one of the oldest sites on the Peruvian coast.

lugares/huaca-pucllana/resumen.texto: An adobe pyramid of the Lima culture, in the present-day Lima district of Miraflores, built with adobe bricks laid in vertical rows like books on a shelf. It contains burials from the Lima culture, including young women interpreted as sacrificed, and later burials from the Wari period.

lugares/tiwanaku/resumen.texto: The capital of the Tiahuanaco culture, south of Lake Titicaca, in present-day Bolivia, with the Akapana pyramid, the semi-subterranean temple, the Kalasasaya with the Gate of the Sun, and the Puma Punku complex, made of stones carved with great precision. In the colonial period and in the 19th and 20th centuries many of its stones were taken for churches, houses and public works, and its chronology became the subject of fantastic theories. It has been a World Heritage Site since 2000.

lugares/huari-sitio/resumen.texto: The capital of the Wari state, near Ayacucho, an extensive city of walled compounds, temples and multi-story underground tombs for the elite, from which provincial centers across much of Peru were controlled.

lugares/pikillacta/resumen.texto: A Wari provincial center in the Lucre valley, near Cusco, with hundreds of orthogonal compounds laid out according to a prior plan. Gordon McEwan interpreted it as an administrative and storage center. It shows that the Cusco valley was under Huari rule or influence centuries before the Incas.

lugares/marcahuamachuco/resumen.texto: A large settlement on top of a plateau in the La Libertad highlands, with galleries and multi-story compounds surrounded by walls. It was the center of the Huamachuco culture before and during the Wari period.

lugares/batan-grande/resumen.texto: A group of adobe pyramids in the La Leche valley, in Lambayeque, capital of the Sicán culture, with very gold-rich elite tombs excavated by Izumi Shimada. It was one of the most looted sites in Peru in the 20th century.

lugares/tucume/resumen.texto: A group of more than twenty adobe pyramids in the Lambayeque valley, occupied by the Sicán, the Chimú and the Incas. Thor Heyerdahl directed excavations between 1988 and 1994. In the Temple of the Sacred Stone, offerings and remains of human sacrifices were found.

lugares/chan-chan/resumen.texto: The capital of the Chimú kingdom, next to present-day Trujillo, the largest adobe city in the Americas, with about ten large walled compounds (ciudadelas) that served as palaces and royal tombs, artisan neighborhoods, and reliefs of fish and birds on the walls. The Incas conquered it around 1470, and the Spanish looted its tombs. It has been a World Heritage Site since 1986.

lugares/kuelap/resumen.texto: A Chachapoya settlement on a ridge at about 3,000 meters, in Amazonas (Peru), surrounded by a wall up to 19 meters high with narrow entrances, and with more than 400 round stone houses with zigzag and diamond friezes. It was inhabited from the mid-first millennium until the colonial period. In 2022 part of its wall collapsed.

lugares/sarcofagos-de-carajia/resumen.texto: A group of anthropomorphic sarcophagi made of clay and cane, more than two meters high, placed by the Chachapoya on a cliff ledge in Amazonas (Peru), with human skulls on top of some of them.

lugares/laguna-de-los-condores/resumen.texto: A lagoon in Amazonas (Peru) with Chachapoya mausoleums on a cliff. In 1997, after an attack by looters, more than 200 funerary bundles and dozens of quipus from the Chachapoya and Inca periods were rescued from it.

lugares/coricancha/resumen.texto: The main temple of Cusco, dedicated to the Sun and other deities, with walls of perfectly fitted stone that witnesses said were covered with gold plates. The ceques radiated from it. In 1533 its gold plates were stripped for Atahualpa’s ransom, and afterward it was given to the Dominicans, who built the church and convent of Santo Domingo on top of it. The earthquakes of 1650 and 1950 exposed its Inca walls.

lugares/sacsayhuaman/resumen.texto: A complex above Cusco with three rows of zigzag walls of large stones fitted without mortar, towers and storehouses. It was begun in Pachacútec’s time and continued by his successors with thousands of rotating workers. The Spanish called it a fortress, and it was the scene of fighting during the siege of Cusco in 1536. Afterward they took stone from it to build the colonial city.

lugares/ollantaytambo/resumen.texto: An Inca town and complex in the Sacred Valley, a royal estate of Pachacútec, with a temple of large porphyry monoliths, terraces, and a grid of blocks that is still inhabited.

lugares/pisac/resumen.texto: An Inca complex above the Sacred Valley, with terraces, temples, neighborhoods and one of the largest known Inca cemeteries, most of which was looted. It is linked to the estates of Pachacútec.

lugares/choquequirao/resumen.texto: An Inca complex in the Vilcabamba range, above the Apurímac River, with terraces decorated with figures of llamas in white stone. It is linked to the estates of Topa Inca and was one of the sites of the Inca state of Vilcabamba.

lugares/raqchi/resumen.texto: An Inca complex south of Cusco with a temple dedicated to the god Viracocha, whose central wall of stone and adobe is more than 90 meters long, and with more than a hundred round storehouses.

lugares/vilcashuaman/resumen.texto: An Inca administrative center in Ayacucho, in the land of the Chanca and Pocra, with a stepped pyramid (ushnu) with a double seat and a temple of the Sun on which a colonial church was built.

lugares/huanuco-pampa/resumen.texto: An Inca administrative center at about 3,800 meters, on the highland royal road, with a large plaza with an ushnu, palaces, an acllawasi and hundreds of storehouses. Excavations by Craig Morris found large quantities of chicha vessels, which indicates a place of feasting and rotating labor more than a city with a permanent population.

lugares/tambo-colorado/resumen.texto: An Inca administrative center of adobe in the Pisco valley, which preserves red and yellow paint on its walls and niches.

lugares/puruchuco/resumen.texto: The palace of a local lord from the Inca period near Lima, where the quipus studied by Gary Urton and Carrie Brezine were found. In the neighboring cemetery of Puruchuco-Huaquerones, more than 2,000 funerary bundles were excavated between 1999 and 2001, among them victims of the siege of Lima in 1536 with the earliest documented firearm wounds in human remains from the Americas.

lugares/tunanmarca/resumen.texto: A walled town of the Huanca on a summit in the Mantaro valley, with thousands of round stone houses, abandoned when the Incas moved its inhabitants to the valleys. It is one of the clearest examples of the wars between lordships that predated the Incas.

lugares/tomebamba/resumen.texto: An Inca city built over the Cañari center of Guapondélig, where Cuenca in Ecuador stands today. According to tradition, Huayna Cápac was born there, and he made it his capital in the north. According to Cieza, it was destroyed in the civil war. Remains survive at Pumapungo.

lugares/ingapirca/resumen.texto: A Cañari and Inca complex in the province of Cañar, Ecuador, with an Inca building of elliptical plan made of finely cut stone, the largest Inca complex in the country.

lugares/pambamarca/resumen.texto: A group of Inca and local fortresses northeast of Quito, dating from Huayna Cápac’s wars against the Cayambe and Caranqui.

lugares/incallajta/resumen.texto: An Inca center in the east of Cochabamba, in present-day Bolivia, with walls and a large storehouse (kallanka), which protected the eastern frontier against the Chiriguano.

lugares/isla-del-sol/resumen.texto: An island in Lake Titicaca where, according to Inca myths, the Sun was born. The Incas built a pilgrimage shrine there next to the sacred rock (Titikala), on top of earlier Tiahuanaco-period worship sites.

lugares/pachacamac/resumen.texto: A shrine on the central coast, south of Lima, home for more than a thousand years to an oracle consulted from afar. It has temples from the Lima culture, the Wari period and the Ichma lordship, and an Inca temple of the Sun and an acllawasi. Max Uhle excavated it in 1896 and found burials of women beside the temple of the Sun, which he interpreted as sacrifices. In 1533 Hernando Pizarro looted it in search of gold for Atahualpa’s ransom and destroyed the oracle’s idol.
